name: Gilbert O'Sullivan
milestone_by_age_26: Topped the US Billboard charts for six weeks with 'Alone Again (Naturally)' in 1972 at age 25, following his first UK Top 10 hit 'Nothing Rhymed' in 1970 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Born Raymond Edward O'Sullivan in Waterford, Ireland in 1946; family emigrated to Swindon, England when he was 7; attended Swindon Art College studying graphic design while playing in semi-professional bands; wrote songs throughout his formative years influenced by The Beatles and Bob Dylan; first three singles on CBS and Major Minor labels flopped before signing with Gordon Mills' MAM Records in 1970.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class Irish family in Waterford; father was a butcher at Clover Meats, mother ran a sweet shop; family emigrated to England when he was 7; father died approximately two years after the move; mother supported his musical interests with piano lessons and instruments.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not in the music industry; mother sent him to piano lessons briefly, but he preferred playing by ear. No documented family domain advantage in music.
primary_early_advantage_tags: songwriting craft, art college, Gordon Mills management, UK pop scene, working-class background, early band playing
evidence_summary: Gilbert O'Sullivan grew up in a working-class Irish immigrant family in Swindon, England, with no music industry connections. He wrote songs throughout his formative years and played in semi-professional bands at art college, including one with Rick Davies (later of Supertramp) who taught him drums and piano. His breakthrough came when he sent demo tapes to Gordon Mills, manager of Tom Jones and Engelbert Humperdinck, who signed him to MAM Records. His distinctive songwriting style, characterized by percussive piano and wordplay, drove his rapid rise from failed singles to UK Top 10 and US #1 hits between 1970 and 1972.
starting_point: Born to a working-class Irish family in Waterford; father was a butcher, mother ran a sweet shop; family emigrated to Swindon, England when he was 7; father died when he was around 9.
current_position: Still active singer-songwriter in his late 70s; released album 'Songbook' in 2024; lives in St Helier, Jersey; continues to tour and record with a career spanning over 55 years.

trajectory.event: Achieved first UK Top 10 hit with 'Nothing Rhymed,' which also reached #1 in the Netherlands, launching his recording career.
'Alone Again (Naturally)' topped the US Billboard charts for six weeks, earning three Grammy nominations and international fame.
Named Songwriter of the Year at the Ivor Novello Awards; had UK #1 hits with 'Clair' and 'Get Down' and album 'Back to Front' topped the UK charts.
Became embroiled in a lengthy legal battle with MAM Records that stalled his career for years.
Won landmark lawsuit against rapper Biz Markie for unauthorized sampling of 'Alone Again (Naturally),' establishing important copyright precedent in hip-hop.
Released self-titled album 'Gilbert O'Sullivan,' his first UK charting studio album in over 40 years, reaching #20 on the UK Albums Chart.
Released 'Songbook,' a critically acclaimed stripped-down re-recording of 12 career-defining songs, and toured internationally.

name: Peter Aerts
milestone_by_age_26: Won the IKBF World Heavyweight Championship at age 19 in 1990, and went on to win the K-1 World Grand Prix tournament in 1994 at age 23 and again in 1995 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Born in Eindhoven, Netherlands in 1970; played football for seven years as a child before starting taekwondo at age 14 in 1983, inspired by his grandfather and uncle who were active in combat sports; transitioned to kickboxing and Muay Thai in 1984, training at Judoka-Kickboxing gym in Best with Eddy Smulders; won his first professional fight after just one year of training; won his first world title at 19 in 1990.
family_context_summary: Born in Eindhoven, Netherlands; played football as a child for seven years; grandfather and uncle were active in combat sports (boxing), which inspired his interest in martial arts; no documented financial privilege.
parent_family_domain_summary: Grandfather was a boxer and uncle was also active in combat sports, though not at a high level; this family connection introduced Aerts to combat sports at age 14.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dutch kickboxing hub, family combat sports, Eddy Smulders training, Thom Harinck Chakuriki Gym, early world title, K-1 rise
evidence_summary: Peter Aerts grew up in Eindhoven, Netherlands, a country that was the global frontier for kickboxing and Muay Thai. His grandfather and uncle were active in boxing, introducing him to combat sports, but he only began training at 14. Within five years, he won his first world title (IKBF Heavyweight Championship at 19), aided by sustained coaching from Eddy Smulders and later Thom Harinck at the renowned Chakuriki Gym in Amsterdam. The Netherlands' dense ecosystem of elite kickboxing gyms and competitors provided the performance pipeline that accelerated his development from novice to world champion in just five years.
starting_point: Born in Eindhoven, Netherlands; played football as a child; grandfather and uncle were active in combat sports (boxing), which inspired his interest in martial arts at age 14.
current_position: Semi-retired kickboxer with estimated net worth of approximately $4 million; last fought professionally in 2020; lives in the Netherlands; involved in gym ownership and training.

trajectory.event: Won the IKBF World Heavyweight Championship against Jan Oosterbaan in Amsterdam, his first world title.
Won the WMTA World Muay Thai Heavyweight Championship by defeating Frank Lobman, adding a second world title.
Won the K-1 World Grand Prix tournament in Tokyo, becoming only the second K-1 champion in history.
Defended K-1 World Grand Prix title, winning the tournament for the second consecutive year.
Won third K-1 World Grand Prix title, stopping all three opponents in a record-setting six minutes and forty-three seconds.
Reached the K-1 World Grand Prix final at age 39, a remarkable late-career achievement.
Had his final professional fight, ending a career spanning over three decades.

He was named Actor of the Year in 1973 at age 32. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Sidney Crosby
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Art Ross Trophy as NHL scoring champion, Hart Memorial Trophy as league MVP, and Lester B. Pearson Award in 2007 at age 19, becoming the youngest scoring champion in any major North American sports league; also scored 102 points as an 18-year-old rookie in 2005-06.
early_history_summary: Born in Halifax, Nova Scotia in 1987; father Troy was a goaltender drafted by the Montreal Canadiens who played in the QMJHL; learned to skate at age 3 and was playing against 10-year-olds by age 6; played AAA minor hockey in Nova Scotia; attended Shattuck-St. Mary's prep school in Minnesota at age 14; played two seasons for Rimouski Océanic in the QMJHL (2003-05), compiling 303 points and twice being named CHL player of the year; selected first overall in the 2005 NHL draft.
family_context_summary: Born to Troy and Trina Crosby in Halifax, Nova Scotia; father Troy was a goaltender drafted 240th overall by the Montreal Canadiens in 1984 who played in the QMJHL; middle-class family with deep hockey involvement; younger sister Taylor; grew up in Cole Harbour.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Troy Crosby was a goaltender who played in the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League and was drafted by the Montreal Canadiens, providing direct hockey domain expertise and mentorship from birth.
primary_early_advantage_tags: hockey prodigy, father goaltender, Shattuck-St. Mary's, QMJHL, early skating, obsessive practice, first overall draft pick
evidence_summary: Sidney Crosby was recognized as a hockey prodigy from age 5, when coaches noted he stuck out 'like a sore thumb' among older children. His father Troy, a former QMJHL goaltender drafted by the Montreal Canadiens, provided direct domain expertise and mentorship from birth, serving as his first goaltender in basement shooting practice. Crosby progressed through the elite hockey pipeline — Nova Scotia minor hockey, Shattuck-St. Mary's prep school in Minnesota, and Rimouski Océanic in the QMJHL — before being selected first overall in the 2005 NHL draft. His legendary work ethic and obsessive concentration on hockey from toddlerhood produced exceptional prior reps, culminating in 102 points as an 18-year-old rookie and the Art Ross, Hart, and Pearson trophies at age 19.
starting_point: Born in Halifax, Nova Scotia to Troy and Trina Crosby; father was a goaltender drafted by the Montreal Canadiens who played in the QMJHL; middle-class family with deep hockey involvement; grew up in Cole Harbour.
current_position: Captain of the Pittsburgh Penguins, signed through 2026-27 season at $8.7M AAV; three-time Stanley Cup champion, two-time Olympic gold medalist; ranks 10th in NHL history with over 1,596 career points.

trajectory.event: Selected first overall in the NHL draft by Pittsburgh Penguins; scored 102 points as a rookie, becoming the youngest player to reach 100 points in NHL history.
Won Art Ross Trophy (scoring champion with 120 points), Hart Trophy (MVP), and Lester B. Pearson Award; youngest scoring champion in major North American sports league history.
Became the youngest captain in NHL history to win the Stanley Cup, leading the Pittsburgh Penguins to the championship.
Won second Art Ross and Hart Trophy; scored the overtime game-winning goal for Canada's Olympic gold medal at Sochi.
Won second Stanley Cup with Pittsburgh and Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP.
Won third Stanley Cup and second consecutive Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP.
Signed two-year contract extension with Penguins through 2026-27 season; continues as one of the NHL's top centers.

name: Katarina Witt
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal at the 1984 Sarajevo Winter Olympics at age 18, followed by her first World Championship title in 1984 and six consecutive European Championships from 1983 to 1988.
early_history_summary: Born in Staaken, East Germany in 1965; mother was a physiotherapist, father directed an agricultural cooperative; began skating at age 5 at the Küchwald ice rink in Karl-Marx-Stadt; talent spotted by coach Bernd Egert who recruited her for the Kinder- und Jugendsportschule (special sports school); began training with legendary coach Jutta Müller at age 10; trained six days a week, up to seven hours a day; first major international competition at 1979 European Championships (age 13); first major podium with silver at 1982 European and World Championships (age 16).
family_context_summary: Born in Staaken, East Germany; mother was a physiotherapist, father directed an agricultural cooperative; grew up in Karl-Marx-Stadt (now Chemnitz); attended the Kinder- und Jugendsportschule, a special school for athletically talented children.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not in figure skating; mother was a physiotherapist and father an agricultural cooperative director. No documented family domain advantage in skating.
primary_early_advantage_tags: East German sports school, Jutta Müller coaching, early skating, intensive training, Küchwald rink, Olympic gold
evidence_summary: Katarina Witt's path to Olympic gold at 18 was shaped by the East German state sports system, which identified her talent at age 5 and placed her in the Kinder- und Jugendsportschule, a special school for athletically talented children. Legendary coach Jutta Müller provided sustained, individualized coaching from age 10, becoming an 'ersatz parent' and training Witt six days a week for up to seven hours a day. The East German sports machine provided elite training facilities, competitive opportunities, and a pipeline of elite peers. Witt's natural talent was recognized early by head coach Bernd Egert, and she progressed from first competition at age 7 to silver medals at European and World Championships at 16, and Olympic gold at 18.
starting_point: Born in Staaken, East Germany; mother was a physiotherapist, father directed an agricultural cooperative; grew up in Karl-Marx-Stadt (Chemnitz); attended a special state sports school for athletically talented children from a young age.
current_position: Retired figure skater turned TV presenter, producer, and activist; lives between Berlin and New York; involved in charitable work and documentary filmmaking; produced documentary about Chemnitz as 2025 European Capital of Culture.

trajectory.event: Won silver medals at both the European and World Figure Skating Championships, her first major international podium finishes.
Won her first European Championship title, beginning a streak of six consecutive European titles.
Won Olympic gold medal at the Sarajevo Winter Olympics and her first World Championship title.
Defended Olympic title at Calgary Winter Olympics with her 'Carmen' program; won fourth World Championship title.
Returned to compete at the Lillehammer Winter Olympics as a professional, finishing seventh but enchanting the crowd.
Inducted into the World Figure Skating Hall of Fame.
Produced and presented documentary 'Chemnitz 2025 – Unterwegs mit Katarina Witt' for the European Capital of Culture celebration.

name: Mick Doohan
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first 500cc Grand Prix at the Hungarian GP in 1990 at age 25, finishing third in the world championship; also won World Superbike Championship races in 1988 at age 23 and made his GP debut with Honda in 1989 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Born in Brisbane, Australia in 1965; youngest of three brothers in a motorcycle-mad family; began riding motorcycles at age 9 in 1974 and competing in off-road dirt bike events; father took the brothers racing on dirt tracks but died when Doohan was 12; family moved to Gold Coast in 1981; made road racing debut in 1984 at age 19 on a Yamaha RZ350 at Surfers Paradise Raceway; worked as a swimming pool concreter before racing full-time; breakthrough in 1987 with international debut at Suzuka 8 Hours; won World Superbike races in 1988; signed by Honda for 500cc GP debut in 1989.
family_context_summary: Born in Brisbane, Australia; youngest of three brothers in a motorcycle-mad family; father took them dirt-track racing but died when Doohan was 12; worked as a swimming pool concreter before pursuing racing full-time; no documented financial privilege.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a motorcycle enthusiast who took his sons dirt-track racing, introducing Doohan to the sport, but was not a professional racer. Father died when Doohan was 12, ending early racing support.
primary_early_advantage_tags: motorcycle family, dirt track racing, self-taught, Honda factory team, Australian racing culture, father's death, concreter background
evidence_summary: Mick Doohan grew up in a motorcycle-mad family in Brisbane and Gold Coast, Australia, beginning dirt-track racing at age 9 with his father and brothers. His father's death when he was 12 ended formal racing support, but Doohan continued riding and transitioned to road racing at 19, working as a concreter to support himself. His natural riding talent was spotted by Japanese Yamaha teams, leading to international debut at the 1987 Suzuka 8 Hours. Honda signed him for the 500cc World Championship in 1989, and he won his first GP at the Hungarian round in 1990 at age 25. His path was largely self-created through obsessive riding from childhood, with limited financial resources and no formal racing academy pipeline.
starting_point: Born in Brisbane, Australia; youngest of three brothers in a motorcycle-mad family; father took them dirt-track racing but died when Doohan was 12; worked as a swimming pool concreter before pursuing racing full-time.
current_position: Aviation entrepreneur and businessman; splits time between Monaco and Gold Coast, Australia; owns Jetcraft Australia, Global Jet International, and Platinum Business Aviation Centre; five-time 500cc World Champion (1994-1998).

trajectory.event: Won World Superbike Championship races in Australia and Japan; won the Australian Motorcycle Grand Prix at Mount Panorama in a breakout season.
Made 500cc Grand Prix debut with Honda factory team; achieved first career podium at the German GP.
Won first 500cc Grand Prix at the Hungarian GP; finished third in the world championship.
Won first 500cc World Championship, beginning a run of five consecutive world titles (1994-1998).
Suffered career-ending crash at Jerez, Spain; retired from motorcycle racing.
Transitioned to aviation business, founding Global Jet International and other aviation ventures after leaving Honda.

name: Nick Price
milestone_by_age_26: Tied for second at the 1982 Open Championship at age 25, one shot behind Tom Watson, after holding a three-shot lead with six holes to play; won his first PGA Tour event at the 1983 World Series of Golf at age 26, beating Jack Nicklaus by four shots.
early_history_summary: Born in Durban, South Africa in 1957 to British parents; father was a career British military officer (Major in artillery); family moved to Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) when Price was 3-5; started caddying for his brother at age 8; grew up playing golf constantly with cheap green fees in Rhodesia; attended Prince Edward School in Salisbury where he captained the golf team; won the Optimist Junior World at Torrey Pines at age 17 in 1974; did military service during the Rhodesian civil war; turned professional in 1977; first professional win at 1979 Asseng TV Challenge Series; won 1980 Swiss Open on European Tour; began working with swing coach David Leadbetter in 1982.
family_context_summary: Born in Durban, South Africa to British parents; father was a career British military officer (Major in artillery) who served in India during WWII; family moved to Rhodesia when Price was 3-5; youngest of three brothers by seven years; grew up during the Rhodesian civil war and did military service.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a career military officer, not in golf; no documented family domain advantage in the sport. Mother and older brother financed his trip to the 1974 Junior World tournament.
primary_early_advantage_tags: caddying start, self-taught swing, Rhodesia golf access, David Leadbetter coaching, military family, junior world win
evidence_summary: Nick Price grew up in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) in a British military family with no golf connections, but the country's cheap green fees and year-round playing weather allowed him to play up to 144 holes a day as a teenager. He started caddying for his brother at age 8 and taught himself golf, winning the Optimist Junior World at 17. After turning pro in 1977, he progressed through the South African and European Tours, with his career accelerating when he began working with childhood friend David Leadbetter as swing coach in 1982. His tied-for-second finish at the 1982 Open Championship at age 25, one shot behind Tom Watson, established him on the world stage, followed by his first PGA Tour win at the 1983 World Series of Golf beating Jack Nicklaus.
starting_point: Born in Durban, South Africa to British parents; father was a career British military officer (Major in artillery); family moved to Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) when Price was 3-5; started caddying for his brother at age 8; grew up during the Rhodesian civil war.
current_position: Retired professional golfer; lives in Hobe Sound, Florida; World Golf Hall of Fame inductee (2003); runs Nick Price Golf Course Design; won three major championships and reached World #1 in 1994.

trajectory.event: Won the Optimist Junior World tournament at Torrey Pines, San Diego, financed by his mother and older brother.
Tied for second at the Open Championship at Troon, one shot behind Tom Watson, after holding a three-shot lead with six holes to play.
Won his first PGA Tour event at the World Series of Golf, beating Jack Nicklaus by four shots wire-to-wire.
Won his first major championship at the PGA Championship, defeating Nick Faldo and others.
Won two majors (The Open Championship and PGA Championship); reached World #1 ranking; named PGA Tour Player of the Year.
Inducted into the World Golf Hall of Fame.
